title: Knee examination
stem: Cubicle 15. Mr Chiu, 26, twisted his right knee playing football yesterday: he heard a pop, could not continue, and the knee swelled within an hour. Examine his knee and explain your findings and plan.
notes:
Checked against the Ottawa knee rule (Stiell 1996), BOA/BASK guidance on acute knee injury, and standard examination technique.

Structure: look (gait, alignment, swelling, effusion, quadriceps wasting, scars), feel (temperature, effusion tests — patellar tap for large effusions, sweep/bulge test for small; joint line tenderness; collateral ligaments; patella), move (active and passive flexion and extension, straight-leg raise to test the extensor mechanism), special tests (Lachman — most sensitive for ACL; anterior drawer; posterior sag and drawer for PCL; valgus and varus stress at 0° and 30° for MCL and LCL; McMurray/Thessaly for menisci with caution in acute pain), and neurovascular status. Examine the hip and the other knee.

An acute haemarthrosis within hours after a twisting injury with a pop: ACL rupture (about 70%), patellar dislocation, osteochondral fracture. Ottawa knee rule for X-ray: age 55 or over, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, cannot flex to 90°, or cannot weight bear 4 steps immediately and in the ED. Management: RICE, analgesia, crutches, brace if needed, early physiotherapy, fracture clinic/knee clinic, MRI. A locked knee (meniscal bucket-handle) needs urgent orthopaedic review.

Your notes list the knee exam headings (look, feel, move, special tests) without detail; nothing conflicts.

Perfect script checked against standard knee examination and the Ottawa knee rule, an HKCEM-style scheme and a keyword scheme. Removed the forceful McMurray and aspirate-every-haemarthrosis options.

Rebuilt as a focused examination (2026-10-12), as the supracondylar station is: every manoeuvre is a button under its heading (look, feel, move, special tests, neurovascular, to complete), shown being done on the patient, with its finding. He lies in football shorts, both legs bare (built for the leg examination: the model's trousers are tucked away). The swelling, the bent knee he keeps, the antalgic gait, the shin sliding forward on the Lachman and his wince on the lateral joint line are on the model. Marks split into single acts: warmth, patellar tap, joint lines and bony points; active and passive movement and the straight-leg raise; pulses, and sensation with power. A passive range with no springy block rules out a locked knee (bucket-handle tear). The common peroneal nerve is checked (foot up and down), as it is at risk in knee injuries. The left Lachman is there to compare and earns nothing on its own.

findings.joint-line@lateraljoint-R: Lateral joint line: tender; he winces.
findings.lachman@knee-L: Left knee: a few millimetres of movement, then a firm end-point. The normal side, for comparison.
findings.touch@foot-R: Feels light touch normally over the foot.

steps.label: Introduce
steps.hint: WIPER: wash hands, introduce, permission, expose both legs, reposition; offer analgesia.

opts.t: Hello, I'm the emergency doctor. I've washed my hands. May I examine your knee? Are you in pain? I can give you something for it.
I need to see both legs from the thighs down, lying on the couch.

steps.label: Examine the knee
steps.hint: Look (gait, both knees), feel (warmth, patellar tap, joint lines, bones), move (active, passive, straight-leg raise), the ligaments (Lachman, posterior drawer, collaterals), then the foot and the hip.

Look.t: Walk a few steps for me, if you can
Look.r: Antalgic gait: four steps, limping, keeping his weight off the right leg. "He can weight-bear four steps."

Look.t: Look at both knees: swelling, bruising, wounds, wasting
Look.r: The right knee is swollen: the hollows beside the patella are filled and the swelling runs up above it. No bruising, wounds or scars; no quadriceps wasting. The left knee is normal.
Look.mark: Inspects both knees for swelling, bruising, wounds and wasting

Feel.t: Feel the temperature of both knees with the back of my hand
Feel.r: The right knee is warm compared with the left.

Feel.t: Patellar tap: empty the pouch above the knee, then tap the kneecap
Feel.r: The patella taps down onto the femur: a positive patellar tap, a large effusion. Swelling within an hour of the injury: a haemarthrosis.

Feel.t: Bend the knee and feel along both joint lines
Feel.r: Tender over the lateral joint line; the medial joint line is not tender.

Feel.t: Press on the patella and the fibular head for bony tenderness
Feel.r: No bony tenderness over the patella or the fibular head.
Feel.mark: Palpates the patella and the fibular head (Ottawa knee rule)

Move.t: Bend your knee up as far as you can, then straighten it
Move.r: He bends it only to 80°, stopped by the tense swelling, and straightens it fully. "He can't flex to 90 degrees."

Move.t: I'll move it for you: a hand on the kneecap, bend and straighten
Move.r: Passively the same, 0 to 80°, painful at the end of flexion; no crepitus; no springy block to straightening, so the knee is not locked.

Move.t: Straight leg raise: keep your knee straight and lift your leg off the bed
Move.r: He lifts the straight leg with no lag: the extensor mechanism is intact.

Special tests.t: Lachman test, knee at 20 to 30 degrees, compared with the other side
Special tests.r: About a centimetre of forward movement of the shin with a soft end-point, more than the left. "A positive Lachman: ACL."

Special tests.t: Posterior sag, then the posterior drawer
Special tests.r: No posterior sag; a firm end-point on the posterior drawer: the PCL is intact.
Special tests.mark: Tests the PCL: posterior sag and drawer

Special tests.t: Valgus and varus stress at 30 degrees and straight
Special tests.r: Stable to valgus and varus stress at 30° and straight: the collateral ligaments are intact.
Special tests.mark: Tests the collateral ligaments at 0° and 30°

Neurovascular.t: Feel the foot pulses: dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial
Neurovascular.r: Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses present.

Neurovascular.t: Light touch on the foot; pull your foot up, then push it down
Neurovascular.r: Light touch normal; he pulls the foot up and pushes it down strongly: the common peroneal and tibial nerves are intact.
Neurovascular.mark: Distal sensation and power (common peroneal nerve)

To complete.t: Roll the leg to examine the hip, the joint above
To complete.r: The hip rolls freely and painlessly: the hip is normal.

steps.ask: Thank you. Please present your findings and your plan.
steps.label: Present and plan
steps.hint: Haemarthrosis with a positive Lachman: likely ACL rupture. Ottawa rule for X-ray. Plan.

opts.t: An acute haemarthrosis with a positive Lachman: likely an ACL rupture; consider a meniscal injury.
Ottawa knee rule: he can't flex to 90 degrees, so a knee X-ray to exclude a fracture, such as a Segond fracture.
Analgesia, ice, crutches, early physiotherapy, knee clinic and an MRI.

script.say: Hello, I'm the emergency doctor. I've washed my hands. May I examine your knee? Are you in pain? I can give you something for it. I need to see both legs from the thighs down, lying on the couch.
Walk a few steps for me, if you can. Look at both knees: swelling, bruising, wounds, wasting.
script.do: Antalgic gait, but he can weight-bear four steps. The right knee is swollen above and beside the patella; no bruising, wounds or wasting.

script.say: Feel the temperature of both knees with the back of my hand. Patellar tap: empty the pouch above the knee, then tap the kneecap. Bend the knee and feel along both joint lines. Press on the patella and the fibular head for bony tenderness.
script.do: Warm compared with the left. A positive patellar tap: a large effusion within an hour, a haemarthrosis. Lateral joint line tender. No bony tenderness at the patella or the fibular head.

script.say: Bend your knee up as far as you can, then straighten it. I'll move it for you: a hand on the kneecap, bend and straighten. Straight leg raise: keep your knee straight and lift your leg off the bed.
script.do: Flexes only to 80°, can't flex to 90 degrees; straightens fully; not locked. Straight leg raise with no lag: extensor mechanism intact.

script.say: Lachman test, knee at 20 to 30 degrees, compared with the other side. Posterior sag, then the posterior drawer. Valgus and varus stress at 30 degrees and straight.
script.do: About a centimetre of forward movement with a soft end-point: a positive Lachman, ACL. No sag, firm posterior drawer. Stable to valgus and varus.

script.say: Feel the foot pulses: dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial. Light touch on the foot; pull your foot up, then push it down. Roll the leg to examine the hip, the joint above.
script.do: Pulses present; sensation and power normal. Hip normal.

script.say: An acute haemarthrosis with a positive Lachman: likely an ACL rupture; consider a meniscal injury. Ottawa knee rule: he can't flex to 90 degrees, so a knee X-ray to exclude a fracture, such as a Segond fracture. Analgesia, ice, crutches, early physiotherapy, knee clinic and an MRI.
